blocks.text: The English scientist Michael Faraday invented a structure in 1836 called the Faraday cage or Faraday shield. A Faraday cage is an enclosure that blocks external electric fields by means of conductive materials. It acts like a hollow conductor in which devices or objects can be put for protection from external electric fields. Any electrical shock received by the cage runs through its outer surface without causing any harm; the electric field inside the hollow conductor remains zero.

blocks.alt: A hollow round conductor placed in the uniform field between a positive top plate and a negative bottom plate. Negative charges gather on the side facing the positive plate and positive charges on the far side. The field lines bend to meet the surface at right angles, and there is no field inside.
blocks.caption: Field lines meet a hollow conductor at right angles (original diagram after Figure 9.19).

blocks.text: To understand how a Faraday cage works, suppose a piece of conductor (say copper) carries a number of excess free electrons. Each electron experiences a force of repulsion because of the electric field of its neighbouring electrons; as a consequence all of them rush to the surface of the conductor. Once static equilibrium is established with all the excess charge on the surface, no further movement of charge occurs. If some electrons shift from the conductor to another object due to friction and so on, a net positive charge appears on the surface of the conductor.

blocks.title: Charge on a conductor
blocks.text: At equilibrium under electrostatic conditions, any excess charge resides on the surface of a conductor.

Now consider the interior of the hollow conductor. The excess charges arrange themselves on the conductor's surface precisely in the manner that the total field within the interior becomes zero. In other words, the conductor shields any charge within it from electric fields outside the conductor. To eliminate the interference of external fields, circuits are often enclosed within metal boxes that provide shielding from such fields.

Figure 9.19 shows another aspect of how conductors alter the electric field lines created by external charges. The lines are altered because the electric field just outside the surface of a conductor is perpendicular to the surface at equilibrium. If the field were not perpendicular, there would be a component of the field parallel to the surface, and the free electrons on the surface would move under it; but in reality no electron flow occurs at equilibrium, so there can be no parallel component, and the field is perpendicular to the surface.

The principle of the Faraday cage demands a material that contains many free electrons that can move freely to its surface. Only conductors have free electrons, whereas insulators do not, so insulators cannot be used to construct a Faraday cage.

items: Cars: the chassis and metal-framed bodies of cars protect the people inside during thunderstorms; the electrical charge travels over the metal surface of the vehicle into the ground.
Microwave ovens: the metal body acts as a Faraday cage and prevents the microwaves from spreading into the environment.
Aeroplanes: when lightning strikes an aeroplane, the electricity is distributed along its metal frame, keeping the passengers and all devices inside safe.
